turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the twenty-second of November, twenty twenty-six. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
It's the Sunday book, so we start with light. A snowbound village in Japan, Shirakawa-go, floodlights its thatched farmhouses on four January nights. By reservation only.
[excited] And the watch! The nineteen fifty-two Patek we said would sell under twenty million Hong Kong dollars made thirty-four point two million.
We were wrong. It's printed as wrong.
[laughs] Graciously. And the rabbit hole is foraging — from a TikTok cookbook to Japan's ten-year ledger of poisonings.
All later. The lead: Iran's foreign minister says the case for dropping its no-bomb doctrine has "strong logic". While insisting nothing has changed.
And the thread through the whole book this Sunday is hours. Who counts them, and who doesn't. Let's go to Tehran.
Abbas Araghchi, in an interview published by the government daily Iran on Saturday the twenty-first. Treaty membership, he said, did not stop Iran's nuclear sites being bombed.
And in the same breath?
"Up to this moment, our doctrine has not changed and our official positions remain the same."
[wry] Both things at once. Very diplomatic. Which treaty, for the rest of us?
The Non-Proliferation Treaty of nineteen seventy. Iran promised never to build or acquire a bomb, in return for the right to peaceful nuclear power. Leaving it is the legal step a bomb would need.
And this lands right on the thing blocking an end to the war.

The war America and Iran have fought since late February. Washington wants a guarantee of no weapon before a full ceasefire. Tehran lists seven conditions first — among them lifting the American naval blockade and freeing its frozen assets.
So the question is the material. Does it exist?

It does. The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates Iran holds four hundred and forty point nine kilograms of uranium enriched to sixty per cent. A weapon needs about ninety. A power station, about three.
[pause] And where is it?

Nobody outside Iran knows. In March the agency's chief, Rafael Grossi, said more than two hundred kilograms was thought to lie in tunnels at Isfahan. In September the agency said it had lost track of the stockpile more than a year before. And inspectors are barred.
[skeptical] So nobody is counting it. What about Iran's friends?
Not on board. "Russia and China are also opposed," he said. Their Shenzhen declaration with America on the nineteenth said a nuclear war cannot be won — and didn't mention Iran.
And from Washington, Donald Trump, answering reports of an Iranian plot against the capital: if they do, "we're going to fight."
The viewpoints. From Doha, on Al Jazeera, Simon Mabon of Lancaster University sees a "broadly rational defensive reason" in Tehran's thinking.
But he warns a defensive shift "can easily be read in offensive terms". His words: "a very, very dangerous moment."

From Prague, Radio Free Europe notes senior security officials and hard-line lawmakers have openly called for leaving the treaty for months. And the stockpile is "one of the biggest unknowns" in any deal.

Rouzbeh Parsi of Lund University says a bomb, once fringe, is now "within the realm of possibility". And J D Vance asks: if you don't want a nuclear weapon, "why do you need sixty percent enriched fuel?"

The sceptic says Iran is bargaining, not building. The fatwa against nuclear arms still stands. Mojtaba Khamenei, supreme leader since March, has stayed out of public view and issued nothing to overturn his father's ruling.
And Zarif's camp argues a weapon would "almost inevitably" bring more strikes. So — ambiguity is leverage at the table.
To the money. And this week's question was simple: when shares fell, where did savers hide?
Gold? Bitcoin?
[deadpan] Neither. American government bonds. The ten-year Treasury yield slid from five point one five to four point nine two per cent over the week.
Okay — mechanism, for those of us who flinch at yields.
A yield is the return someone buying today locks in. When buyers crowd in, it falls. So a falling yield means people were piling into bonds.
And bitcoin?

Its funds lost one point two five billion US dollars in the five days to Friday — the third week running above a billion. Bitcoin itself has fallen seven weeks in a row, to about sixty thousand three hundred and twenty dollars late on Saturday.
But gold's the puzzle, isn't it? Gold should love falling real yields.

It should. It pays no interest, so it gains when cash pays less. Instead — [pause] it fell eight per cent in three sessions, from three thousand eight hundred and fifty-three dollars on Tuesday to a Friday close of three thousand five hundred and thirty-eight.
Why?
Investors sold winners to cover losses on shares. The desk calls Friday a forced sale, not a verdict on real yields.
[curious] So does the desk's standing call survive?

[wry] The real-rate shock — the Federal Reserve tightening. Held since issue one sixty-two, and nothing has tripped. It changes if the ten-year real yield closes under two point six, if there's no rise on the ninth of December, or if the junk-bond spread tops four points. It's at three point five two.
And the four leans fall due on Wednesday.

The four from issue one sixty-six were all on course at Friday's close. This week's leans: the all-world fund, V W R A, lower. PIMCO Income, steady to slightly up. Gold, lower while the dollar stays firm. Bitcoin, lower.

And the sceptic is a survey. The University of Michigan's consumer survey, run by Joanne Hsu: households' expected inflation a year out fell. So part of that Treasuries rally was cooler prices, not just fear.

And the slow money, on page fifteen: the World Gold Council counts six hundred and seventy-five tonnes of central-bank gold in the first nine months of the year. [deadpan] All of this is explanation, not investment advice.
Noted. Now Singapore — the Prime Minister was in Beijing.
Lawrence Wong met Premier Li Qiang on Saturday. Ministers signed a transport pact and a green-industry pact. Li promised to "accelerate negotiations" on upgrading the free-trade agreement.
And there's an A I piece.

Singapore's A I Verify testing framework was mapped line by line against a Chinese standard, showing which safeguards correspond. That should spare firms selling A I in both markets some duplicated effort.
And the sceptic?

A mapping is a table, not mutual recognition. Firms still answer to two regulators. And Xinhua's version has Wong backing Xi's "four global initiatives" — a line absent from Singapore's own statement. For your diary: Singapore's October consumer prices on Monday, and the Economic Survey on Tuesday at eight in the morning.
Technology. T S M C has shut a door.
Reuters reported on the nineteenth that T S M C told Chinese chip designers to stop ordering from its better production lines unless they hold an American export licence. T S M C hasn't confirmed it.
Better lines meaning smaller numbers.

Chips are graded by their finest features, in nanometres. Smaller is faster and more frugal. Until the nineteenth some Chinese A I designers could still order at seven. The line now sits at sixteen. Without a licence, they're generally held to twenty-eight and forty.
So investors —

— priced it fast. Its New York shares fell two point nine three per cent that day, to their lowest since April. Lines at seven nanometres and finer earned seventy-nine per cent of third-quarter wafer revenue. [deadpan] But it doesn't publish China sales, so the lost orders can't be sized.

The sceptic says T S M C loses little. October sales rose fifty-nine point seven per cent on a year earlier, and blocked designers will probably shift work to Chinese foundries. Right — the Kit. Grado has finally cut the cord on open-back headphones.
[amused] The G W two hundred. Three hundred and twenty-nine US dollars, shipping in December. More than sixty hours a charge, and it plays through a wire when the battery's flat.
Open-back means the cups breathe. Lovely sense of space. But sound leaks both ways — so a quiet study, not a train.

[skeptical] Two cautions. The sources disagree on whether there's a microphone. And Grado's store ships only to American addresses; no Singapore price. Its own wired S one fifty costs two hundred and ninety-five US dollars, and no one had published a listening test by press.
And the Atelier's maker of the day — chopsticks.

Hyozaemon, in Obama, in Fukui. Its hand-shaved kezuri pair, in natural urushi, costs five thousand five hundred yen. And it re-lacquers worn tips, from one thousand one hundred yen, in one to two months.
[warmly] I love that. You send your chopsticks home for a rest. But the chairman's own warning: most lacquered chopsticks on sale use plastic-based paint, not urushi, the sap of the lacquer tree.
The sceptic: past a hand-shaved body and a urushi tip the maker will renew, money buys the box and the painting. Not a longer life.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Into a hedge, I assume.
Into a hedge! Foraging. Find a plant, be certain what it is, take a little, cook it. Older than farming. Mushrooms are a separate tribe — this is greens, seaweed, fruit, nuts and flowers.
And it has a new loudest teacher.

Alexis Nikole Nelson. The Black Forager. Thirty-four, from Ohio, foraging since twenty fifteen. Four point nine million followers on TikTok. And this September, a cookbook called "Happy Snacking, Don't Die!"
[amused] The whole hobby in four words. Where may you pick?

Depends on the country. Sweden is the dream — allemansrätten, the right of public access. Anyone may pick wild flowers and berries on other people's land, "in moderation", but never dig up whole plants.
And Singapore is the hard case.

[sighs] It is. Trees and their fruit on state land belong to the state, and picking — even taking fallen fruit — needs permission from the National Parks Board. Without it, a fine of up to five thousand dollars in a public park; up to fifty thousand, or six months in jail, in a nature reserve or national park.
[wry] So what's the legal route here?
Guided walks. The Parks Board runs free edible-garden tours at the Chinese Garden in Jurong Lake Gardens. And last year the Heritage Festival ran "Hidden Roots", a tasting walk led by Alexius Yeo.
Then the gear. I can hear you getting excited.

[excited] The knife is where the ladder starts. Entry is French: Opinel's number eight folding knife in carbon steel, twenty-three US dollars. For roots and stubborn stems, the hori-hori — a Japanese digging knife, one plain edge, one serrated.
[curious] And the buy-once one?
Niwaki's Hori Hori Pro, handmade by third-generation craftsmen in Miki, in Hyogo. Carbon steel, a one-hundred-and-seventy-millimetre blade. Forty-four pounds in Kew's shop.
Which ships only within Britain. Against a signature and an age check.
[laughs] For a trowel! Then the basket. The Sussex trug — a rim of hand-split sweet chestnut, shaved willow boards, copper nails so nothing rusts. A trug-maker is on record in fourteen eighty-five.
And there's a royal footnote.

Thomas Smith of Herstmonceux showed his at the Great Exhibition of eighteen fifty-one, and Queen Victoria bought several. Labour and Wait sells one handmade in Herstmonceux for a hundred and sixty pounds.
[deadpan] Out of stock online, naturally.

Naturally. [excited] But the real endgame is books. Sam Thayer's twenty twenty-three field guide runs seven hundred and thirty-six pages, thirty-two dollars ninety-five. His first book has sold three hundred thousand copies, by his publisher's count.
The desk's sound first kit: the Opinel and the Thayer guide. About fifty-six US dollars. A hand-made trug costs more than both.

And the phone? A twenty twenty-three Irish test of six identification apps on thirty-eight wild plants. Pl at Net named eighty-eight point two one per cent correctly from flowers. Google Lens, sixty-seven point eight six. And iNaturalist scored three point five seven per cent at species level —
[wry] — because it usually stops at the genus. The authors' verdict: treat apps as "an aid to plant identification".
Which is the bridge to the dark part. The mistakes.
Look-alikes. And the carrot family is where they kill.
[thoughtful] Poison hemlock. Smooth, hollow stems spotted or streaked with purple, hairless leaves, a mousy smell. Wild carrot has hairy stems and no purple. Harmless cow parsley lacks the spots.
Six to eight fresh hemlock leaves can kill an adult. There's no antidote. [pause] It was the poison of Socrates.

And Japan keeps the ledger. From twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-five, its health ministry counted two hundred and eighteen poisonings from wild or garden plants. Six hundred and eighty-eight people ill. Seventeen dead.

And the culprits are a surprise. The daffodil caused the most — seventy-four incidents, two hundred and twenty-seven patients — picked in mistake for garlic chives. Autumn crocus: only twenty-two incidents. [pause] But thirteen of the deaths.

[exhales] Thirteen. And last year alone, seventeen incidents, forty people ill, one death. Most of the patients elderly. And in the mountains, bears killed thirteen people in the year to March — a record.
Give me some vocabulary to survive a dinner party with.
Sansai — Japan's wild "mountain vegetables". Nira — garlic chives, the daffodil's deadly twin. Ramsons — wild garlic. And umbellifer — the carrot family, flat umbrella flowers. Hemlock's tribe.
And the case against.
Brussels bans wild-garlic picking in its forests. Their environment agency says removing the plant removes the reproductive part, and at scale "it can lead to the extinction of this species."
And the forager's own ethic?
[warmly] Mark Williams, of Galloway Wild Foods. "If you can't tell you have been there, you are doing it well."

[chuckles] Fine. That one I like. Back to the surface — the watch. Lot nine five eight, at Phillips in Hong Kong. A nineteen fifty-two Patek Philippe twenty-four ninety-nine in yellow gold. Thirty-four million one hundred and seventy-five thousand Hong Kong dollars with premium. About four point four million US.
[gasps] Against an estimate of twelve to twenty-four million.
And against this book's call: inside the estimate, under twenty. It ran fourteen million past that line. [pause] The call was wrong.
Why did it run?

Freshness. It hadn't been offered in public since nineteen eighty-nine; buyers paid for a watch nobody had picked over. The sceptic: one lot needs only two determined bidders. Today's session runs from eleven in the morning.

Quick one from the cinema. Sunrise on the Reaping took fifty-six million US dollars in North America on Friday. Issue one sixty-nine carried TheWrap's call of an opening above a hundred million — but the weekend number is still a projection. Held, still open.
The family desk, briefly. A study of eleven thousand eight hundred and sixty-eight American children, interviewed separately from their parents.
And they mostly disagree. Depending on the condition and the age, a diagnosis came from only one of the two in roughly sixty-five to ninety-eight per cent of cases.
Children report the inward things — depression, sleep trouble, self-injury. Parents report what shows — conduct, eating, anxiety.
[warmly] So for a girl of twelve about to start secondary school: ask her directly, and on her own, about sleep and mood.
Don't be alarmist, though. Another researcher's pooled work says a gap carries information — not proof a parent has missed something. General guidance, not medical advice.
And to the snow. Shirakawa-go in January.
Four evenings in twenty twenty-seven. Monday the eleventh, a public holiday. Then Sundays the seventeenth, twenty-fourth and thirty-first. Lit from half past five to half past seven in the evening.
And nobody gets in without a booking.
A gate closes the village from half past three. Ticket-holders wear a lanyard pass, colour-coded by date. None are sold on the day.

So the routes in. Returned village rooms go on sale first-come on the twenty-sixth of November, one in the afternoon Japan time. The second car-park round opens on the first of December, seven thousand yen a car.

Winter tyres required, no changes, no refunds. The famous view from the observation deck comes only with a village room or a bus tour. [pause] And a village survey found fifty-nine point four per cent of residents with a negative impression of foreign tourists. The tourism association's chairman is reported as saying it's nearing its limit.
[thoughtful] Gokayama's villages, on the Toyama side, carry the same roofs with smaller crowds. And Takayama, two hours away by bus, is the warmer base.
One last house note. Sunday's book carries the week in review, on page twenty-nine.
The Reader's Editor grading us.

[deadpan] Headlines shortened, from eleven point eight words to nine. Photographs rose from ten to eighteen. But the outside reader's mean score fell, from four point oh nine to three point seven three. Sixteen held items settled; forty-four still open.
[chuckles] Shorter isn't automatically better. Noted. Okay — the Undercurrent. Let's slow right down.
In the first week of November, high schools across Nanjing moved their gates by half an hour.
[warmly] And parents posted the new timetables online as if they were exam results.
One wrote: "We used to be in class at six forty and out of evening study at nine thirty. Now it is seven fifteen and nine twenty."
Another: "Our evening study finishes ten minutes early!" [pause] Ten minutes. With an exclamation mark.
Reporters for Jiangsu's live government phone-in found high schoolers on campus about fifteen hours a day. Arriving around half past six. Leaving after ten at night.
And on air, the province's education director, Jiang Yong, said he felt "deeply guilty".
He conceded the hours harm students' health. The province had run twelve rounds of inspections this year. "Without students' physical and mental health, nothing else is worth discussing."
How long is the week, in total?

[pause] Peking University's twenty twenty-two panel study: an average of sixty-eight point six hours a week for high-school students. At the elite key schools, a twenty twenty-six study found seventy-five point one.
[exhales] Sixty-eight hours a week. For teenagers.
And here's the part that stings. None of it was legal to begin with. Jiangsu's twenty twenty-four rules already barred middle-school lessons before eight and evening study after half past nine.
So how did schools get round it?
[wry] By renaming. "Morning reading" became pre-class preparation, or self-study. The rule fixed the hour of the first lesson; the schools moved the work to hours with another name.
[thoughtful] So the fight over the school day is really a fight over what counts as school.
And why the day grew so long is institutional. One commentator called it a prisoner's dilemma. In a contest for university places, no school wants to be the first to cut hours.
And the children's sleep carries the cost. Nearly forty-two per cent of eleven-year-olds sleep too little.
[thoughtful] Look at that Nanjing parent's figures again. Thirty-five minutes gained at dawn. Ten at night. A day of fourteen hours fifty became fourteen hours five.
[pause] And a researcher warns that if the total workload isn't cut, evening study will simply grow to absorb the morning.

Britain fought the same fight over a different child. The Factory Act of eighteen thirty-three held young people under eighteen to twelve hours a day. Mill owners answered with the "false relay" — cutting the same children's hours into pieces scattered across a longer day.
So no inspector could tell from the clock who'd worked how long.
The Act of eighteen fifty stopped counting hours and fixed a window. Women and young persons could work only between six in the morning and six at night. All work ended at two on Saturday.
[thoughtful] And it actually lengthened the legal week. Britain had tried a weekly cap of fifty-eight hours, and the mills cut it into relays. The window allowed sixty.
[pause] The reformers gave up two hours to get a rule an inspector could check from the street.
One inspector put it plainly. A mill working past its hours gave itself away, because "the lights in the window will discover the one but not the other."
Jiangsu's new start times are half a window. A gate opens at seven twenty or it doesn't. Every parent can see which.
The closing half is where the hours live.
[warmly] The essay's suggestion: one closing time for evening study, the same at every school in a city, visible from the gate. It would do more than any reform of the morning.
And the desk's expectation?
Jiangsu won't bring its half-past-nine limit forward before the twenty twenty-seven gaokao opens on the seventh of June. The gates will move. The evening lights will not.
[warmly] Where the change has held, a father in Hefei says his child sleeps nearly an hour longer… and eats breakfast without rushing.
Bertrand Russell, on our contents page. "The wise use of leisure, it must be conceded, is a product of civilization and education."
[pause] In Lancashire the evidence was a lit mill window after six. In Nanjing, it's a lit classroom after half past nine.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — thirty pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
